slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: Proving a backport with git branch --contains <original ID>. Root cause: the copy is a new commit with a new ID and no link to the original; ancestry knows nothing about it.
Picking without -x between public branches. Root cause: no field of the commit object points to the original, so the message line is the only link that travels with the history.
Using -n and committing with -m. Root cause: with -n no cherry-pick is in progress, so the commit gets you as author; git commit -C <original> restores message and authorship.
Believing that -m 1 on a merge commit merges the branch. Root cause: the result has one parent, so the branch's commits are still unmerged and a later real merge adds them next to the copy.
Expecting A..B to include A. Root cause: the range is "reachable from B and not from A"; A^..B includes it.

beats.text: Both statements can be true at the same time. To see how, you need to know one thing about cherry-pick that the name hides: nothing is picked up and carried over. A change is recomputed, and a new commit is written. Git keeps no link between the two. Keep both statements in mind. They come back.

beats.text: The textbook's statement of the central fact: a cherry-pick does not move or reuse a commit. It recomputes the change that a commit made and records that change as a new commit, with a new ID, on the branch you are on. Git stores no link between the original and the copy. A commit, remember, is one saved snapshot of the project, and a branch is a name that points at one commit.
beats.tele: The textbook's statement of the central fact: a cherry-pick does not move or reuse a commit. A commit, remember, is one saved snapshot of the project, and a branch is a name that points at one commit.

beats.text: So there are two things to learn. How the change is recomputed: as a three-way merge, which combines two versions against a common base, and with a base you might not expect. And what the new commit shares with the original: less than you would think.

beats.text: In one sentence: git cherry-pick <commit> 🟡 CAUTION takes the difference between a commit and its parent, merges that difference into your current branch with a three-way merge, and commits the result.
beats.tele: In one sentence: `git cherry-pick <commit>` 🟡 CAUTION takes the difference between a commit and its parent, merges that difference into your current branch with a three-way merge, and commits the result.

beats.text: Precisely. A cherry-pick is a three-way merge with an unusual choice of base. Call the picked commit C and its parent P. On screen, C is f98ffd3 on main, P is ca6dd48, one step before it, and HEAD, where you are, is release/1.4.
beats.tele: Precisely. A cherry-pick is a three-way merge with an unusual choice of base. Call the picked commit C and its parent P. On screen, C is `f98ffd3` on `main`, P is `ca6dd48`, one step before it, and HEAD, where you are, is `release/1.4`.

beats.text: The merge computes "what changed from P to C" and "what changed from P to HEAD" and combines the two. Whatever else exists on C's branch plays no part.
beats.tele: The merge computes "what changed from P to C" and "what changed from P to HEAD" and combines the two. Whatever else exists on C's branch plays no part.

beats.text: Compare with the revert from the undo module, the commit that undoes another commit. There the base was the commit itself and theirs was its parent. A cherry-pick is the mirror image: base is the parent, theirs is the commit. Same machinery, inputs swapped.
beats.tele: Compare with the revert from the undo module, the commit that undoes another commit. There the base was the commit itself and theirs was its parent. A cherry-pick is the mirror image: base is the parent, theirs is the commit. Same machinery, inputs swapped.

beats.text: Why is "it applies a patch" imprecise? A patch is a change written out as a diff. It carries a few lines of context and fails when they don't match. The merge works with three complete versions of each file. You'll see a change that is refused as a patch and succeeds as a cherry-pick.
beats.tele: Why is "it applies a patch" imprecise? A patch is a change written out as a diff. It carries a few lines of context and fails when they don't match. The merge works with three complete versions of each file. You'll see a change that is refused as a patch and succeeds as a cherry-pick.

beats.text: Inside .git: one new commit object, with new tree and blob objects where content is new. The current branch ref advances by one commit, and the HEAD reflog, the local list of where HEAD has been, gets an entry that starts with cherry-pick:. ORIG_HEAD is not written. While a pick is stopped, the root ref CHERRY_PICK_HEAD names the commit being picked. That's the next video.

The current branch ref advances by one commit, and the HEAD reflog, the local list of where HEAD has been, gets an entry that starts with `cherry-pick:`. `ORIG_HEAD` is not written. While a pick is stopped, the root ref `CHERRY_PICK_HEAD` names the commit being picked. That's the next video.

beats.text: The new commit. It shares the author, the author date and the message with the original, and nothing else. A different tree, a different parent and a different committer line, the line for whoever created this commit object, give a different hash. And no field points from the copy to the original.

beats.tele: The options.

beats.text: -x records where the change came from: it appends the line "(cherry picked from commit", the full ID, to the message. That line is the only link between copy and original that travels with the history. The manual's advice is to use it between publicly visible branches and not for commits from a private branch, whose IDs mean nothing to anyone else.

beats.text: -e opens the editor on the message.
beats.tele: `-e` opens the editor on the message.

beats.text: -n 🟡 applies the change without committing.
beats.tele: `-n` 🟡 applies the change without committing.

beats.text: -m <parent-number> is required for a merge commit, because "the difference between a commit and its parent" is ambiguous when there are two parents.
beats.tele: `-m <parent-number>` is required for a merge commit, because "the difference between a commit and its parent" is ambiguous when there are two parents.

beats.text: Others in brief, from the textbook: -s adds a Signed-off-by trailer, -S signs the new commit, -X passes an option to the merge machinery, and --ff fast-forwards instead of copying when HEAD already is the parent of the picked commit.
beats.tele: Others in brief, from the textbook: `-s` adds a `Signed-off-by` trailer, `-S` signs the new commit, `-X` passes an option to the merge machinery, and `--ff` fast-forwards instead of copying when HEAD already is the parent of the picked commit.

beats.text: Several commits and ranges. Given several commits, cherry-pick copies them one after the other. Given a range, it copies the commits of the range from oldest to newest. Commits that you list are applied in the order you list them. A range A..B means "reachable from B and not from A", so A itself is not included. Write A^..B to include it.
beats.tele: Several commits and ranges. Given several commits, cherry-pick copies them one after the other. Given a range, it copies the commits of the range from oldest to newest. Commits that you list are applied in the order you list them. A range `A..B` means "reachable from B and not from A", so A itself is not included. Write `A^..B` to include it.

beats.text: When not to cherry-pick? When a merge would do. A pick creates a second commit for the same change, and the module's third video is about what that costs.
beats.tele: When not to cherry-pick? When a merge would do. A pick creates a second commit for the same change, and the module's third video is about what that costs.

beats.text: The textbook's analogy: a colleague edited another copy of a document with change tracking on. You don't paste their paragraph over yours. You ask what they changed, compared with what they started from, and make that change in your copy, which has drifted in the meantime.
beats.tele: The textbook's analogy: a colleague edited another copy of a document with change tracking on. You don't paste their paragraph over yours. You ask what they changed, compared with what they started from, and make that change in your copy, which has drifted in the meantime.

beats.text: It breaks at judgment. A person notices when the change refers to a definition that exists only in the other copy. Git does not: the change applies, and your document is now wrong. That's the second of the CTO's questions in this chapter, "the backport applied without a single conflict, and the build broke anyway". A backport is a fix copied from the development line to a maintenance line. And this is the semantic conflict from the merge module in a new costume.

beats.text: The textbook also gives you a rule for which model of a commit to use when. "A commit is a diff" is the right model for predicting what a cherry-pick does. "A commit is a snapshot with parents" is the right model for understanding what it leaves behind. On screen is what it leaves behind: two commits, and no line between them.

beats.text: Step 4: what it demands of your working tree. labs/run ch10/pick-dirty. The manual says the working tree must be clean. Git 2.55 is more precise than that. Three cases. An unstaged edit in a file the pick doesn't touch. An unstaged edit in the file it changes. And a staged change in an untouched file. Try it now, on paper. Thirty seconds: for each, write "goes through" or "refused".

beats.text: Case one goes through: an unstaged edit in a file the pick does not write is left alone.
beats.tele: Case one goes through: an unstaged edit in a file the pick does not write is left alone.

beats.text: Case two is refused: an unstaged edit in a file it must write stops the command.

beats.text: Case three is refused too: any staged change stops it, even in a file the pick doesn't touch.

beats.text: Most people miss that one. In both refusals the command stops before it does anything, and nothing is lost.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Proving a backport with git branch --contains <original ID>. Root cause: the copy is a new commit with a new ID and no link to the original; ancestry knows nothing about it.
beats.tele: Proving a backport with `git branch --contains <original ID>`. Root cause: the copy is a new commit with a new ID and no link to the original; ancestry knows nothing about it.

beats.text: Picking without -x between public branches. Root cause: no field of the commit object points to the original, so the message line is the only link that travels with the history.
beats.tele: Picking without `-x` between public branches. Root cause: no field of the commit object points to the original, so the message line is the only link that travels with the history.

beats.text: Using -n and committing with -m. Root cause: with -n no cherry-pick is in progress, so the commit gets you as author; git commit -C <original> restores message and authorship.
beats.tele: Using `-n` and committing with `-m`. Root cause: with `-n` no cherry-pick is in progress, so the commit gets you as author; `git commit -C <original>` restores message and authorship.

beats.text: Believing that -m 1 on a merge commit merges the branch. Root cause: the result has one parent, so the branch's commits are still unmerged and a later real merge adds them next to the copy.
beats.tele: Believing that `-m 1` on a merge commit merges the branch. Root cause: the result has one parent, so the branch's commits are still unmerged and a later real merge adds them next to the copy.

beats.text: Expecting A..B to include A. Root cause: the range is "reachable from B and not from A"; A^..B includes it.

beats.text: And the warning that goes with both. A clean cherry-pick is a new snapshot that nobody has run. The fix on main may call a helper that was introduced two commits earlier on main and does not exist on the release line. The pick applies. The release is broken. Git has compared text in three versions of the files the commit touched, and nothing else. Run the release branch's tests after every pick, as you would after any merge.
